subject: Banking
title: Did QE Cause Inequality?
description: One-minute skill: Did QE Cause Inequality?.

hook.text: After QE, US household wealth rose $40 trillion. But 70% went to the richest 20% who owned stocks and property.

buildup.text: QE works by raising asset prices. If you own assets, you get richer. If you don't, you watch others pull ahead.

discovery.text: Home prices rose 40% during QE. First-time buyers were priced out while homeowners gained hundreds of thousands.

twist.text: Central banks say QE was necessary to prevent depression.

climax.text: QE saved the economy but widened the gap. The monetary medicine worked for the system but the side effects were unequal.

punchline.text: $40 trillion in new wealth. 70% went to the richest fifth of America.

quiz.question: Who benefited most from quantitative easing?

details.summary: Quantitative easing boosted asset prices for stocks, bonds, and real estate, primarily benefiting wealthy owners of those assets. Critics argue QE widened the wealth gap while providing limited benefits to ordinary workers.
details.whyItMatters: If central bank policy itself creates inequality, it undermines the social contract. Understanding QE's distributional effects is crucial for designing monetary policies that do not concentrate wealth.
takeaways: QE inflated asset prices, directly benefiting existing asset owners
The wealthiest 10 percent own the vast majority of financial assets
Central banks argue QE also preserved jobs and prevented deflation

faq.question: How did quantitative easing increase inequality?
faq.answer: By purchasing bonds and pushing interest rates down, QE drove investors into stocks and real estate, boosting prices. Since the wealthy own the most assets, they captured the largest gains while wage earners saw little direct benefit.

faq.question: Do central banks acknowledge QE's inequality effects?
faq.answer: Some officials acknowledge the trade-off. The Bank of England published research showing QE disproportionately benefited the wealthy. Central banks argue the alternative of doing nothing during a crisis would have hurt the poor more through mass unemployment.
